strengths: Significance: Automatically initializing and recovering 6D object tracking from a supplied CAD model addresses a useful robotics problem. Combining segmentation with failure detection could reduce deployment effort and persistent tracking drift.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports improved pose AR over FoundationPose + CNOS on LM-O (0.41 to 0.53) and YCB-Video (0.69 to 0.74). Table 3 reports a substantial tracking AR improvement on modified YCB-Video (50.09 to 67.85). These results suggest that automatic recovery can materially improve the underlying tracker.

Originality: The particular integration of multi-view attention, semantic conditioning, and memory-based tracking verification is a plausible systems contribution. Table 4 provides supporting evidence for the attention-based verifier, improving classification accuracy from 95.23% without attention to 98.36% with one layer.

Presentation: The SOM/TOM decomposition and Figure 2 make the overall pipeline understandable. The appendix provides useful architectural pseudocode, augmentation settings, and ablations on language conditioning and attention depth.
weaknesses: Soundness—central supervision claims are contradicted or unexplained. The abstract claims operation without additional training, while Section 4 describes extensive SOM and TOM training. More seriously, SOM is described as entirely label-free, but Equation 2 requires ground-truth pixel labels and Appendix D explicitly transforms query images with corresponding masks. No pseudo-label generation procedure explains their source. TOM explicitly uses BOP ground-truth masks and object identities to construct training pairs. Annotation-free initialization at deployment is plausible, but the stronger supervision-free characterization and comparisons across supervision levels are not established.

Soundness—generalization and evaluation splits are insufficiently specified. SOM trains on subsets of the same named BOP datasets used for evaluation, without an object-disjoint protocol demonstrating novel-object generalization. The tracking-pair dataset lacks a documented train/validation/test partition, including separation of source frames, sequences, objects, and memory crops. Consequently, the 98.36% classification accuracy cannot establish performance on independent tracking failures. This is an unresolved evaluation issue, not evidence that leakage occurred.

Evaluation reliability: Appendix B defines AP as an average of precision values across IoU thresholds, omitting precision–recall integration; it is unclear whether the implementation actually uses standard AP. Table 1 labels its quantities ADD and ADD-S although the reported values and interpretation appear to concern success rates; the precise aggregation protocol is unclear. Section 4 also claims state-of-the-art segmentation on four datasets, including T-LESS, whereas Table 2 shows STORM at 47.1 versus 72.1 for ZebraPose and several higher unsupervised scores. Baseline provenance and matching evaluation settings need clarification.

Tracking evidence does not isolate the proposed recovery mechanism sufficiently. The frame-dropping and synthetic-occlusion distributions, evaluation sample counts, and repeated-run variability are unspecified. Comparison against FoundationPose without recovery does not establish an advantage over periodic re-detection or a simple confidence-triggered recovery baseline. Pair-classification accuracy also does not directly measure detection of incorrect 6D poses for the correct object. Failure precision/recall, recovery latency, and performance under sustained disappearance would strengthen the central tracking claim.

Reproducibility is materially weakened by conflicting implementation details. Section 4 specifies AdamW for both modules and 15 TOM epochs, while Appendix D specifies SGD for SOM and Adam with 10 epochs for TOM. Equation 2 uses a two-term Tversky/focal objective with weights and parameters that differ substantially from Appendix D's four-term loss. Input resolutions, backbone variants, failure thresholds, memory management, and pose-estimation sensor requirements are not sufficiently specified. The abstract's 'Code:' field is empty, leaving no accessible implementation to resolve these discrepancies.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence. SOM takes 0.183 seconds per image in Table 2, while language-enabled SOM takes 0.265 seconds in Table 5; Table 3 reports 98 milliseconds for tracking. These measurements do not establish end-to-end real-time recovery because the accounting for rendering, language generation, segmentation, and pose re-registration is unclear. Recovery frequency and latency distributions are needed to substantiate performance during the challenging conditions emphasized by the paper.

Originality and limitations: Most components are established techniques, and combining focal and Tversky losses alone does not substantiate a novel loss contribution. Existing ablations do not separate the benefits of hierarchical fusion, ordinary cross-attention, and additional model capacity. The conclusion lists future directions but offers little analysis of incorrect memory updates, prolonged occlusion, or semantic ambiguity. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark work; the decisive barriers to acceptance are unsupported central claims and inadequate experimental reproducibility.

strengths: Significance: Automatic mask initialization and recovery after tracking failure address useful deployment problems. Combining these capabilities with FoundationPose could reduce manual intervention in model-based object tracking.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports substantial improvements over CNOS + FoundationPose on LM-O, including AR increasing from 0.41 to 0.53. Table 3 reports improved AR on modified YCB-Video from 50.09 to 67.85. These results motivate further investigation.

Originality: The combination of multi-view feature fusion, semantic conditioning, and a memory-based failure detector constitutes a potentially useful systems contribution. Table 4 provides evidence that learned matching improves the constructed classification task, with attention increasing accuracy from 95.23% to 98.36%.
Presentation: The SOM/TOM decomposition and pipeline diagram make the overall approach understandable. The appendix supplies algorithmic descriptions, augmentation settings, and component ablations.
weaknesses: Soundness—central supervision claims are unsupported and internally contradictory. Section 4 and Appendix C describe SOM as entirely label-free, but Equations 2–3 require ground-truth pixel labels and Appendix D explicitly transforms corresponding masks during training. No pseudo-label generation procedure explains this discrepancy. TOM explicitly uses BOP ground-truth masks to construct training pairs. Annotation-free deployment is plausible, but this does not establish supervision-free training or the abstract's claim of operating without additional training.

Soundness—novel-object generalization and comparison fairness are not established. SOM is trained on subsets of datasets that also supply the evaluation benchmarks, without sufficiently specifying training images, object overlap, or held-out-object protocols. This does not prove leakage, but it prevents verification of the zero-shot and generalization claims and complicates comparison against methods categorized as requiring zero retraining.

Evaluation validity: Appendix B defines AP as precision averaged over IoU thresholds, omitting integration over the precision–recall curve. It is unclear whether the implementation uses standard BOP/COCO evaluation or this nonstandard definition. Table 1 labels its quantities mean ADD and ADD-S, although the interpretation appears to require thresholded recall rather than distances; the exact aggregation is unspecified. The text also claims state-of-the-art segmentation on four datasets including T-LESS, whereas Table 2 shows STORM at 47.1 versus 72.1 for ZebraPose.

Tracking evidence is incomplete. Random frame dropping and masking are reasonable stress tests, but their distributions and severity are unspecified. The classification dataset lacks a clear train/test split and sequence/object separation. Moreover, matching object identity does not necessarily detect an incorrect 6D pose when the crop still contains the correct object. Recovery latency, false-trigger rates, and performance against periodic re-registration or simpler confidence-triggered recovery are needed to establish the detector's practical advantage.

Reproducibility is materially weakened by conflicting specifications. The main text uses AdamW for both modules and 15 TOM epochs; Appendix D specifies SGD for SOM and Adam with 10 epochs for TOM. The appendix also changes the segmentation loss components and weights from Equations 2–3. Important architecture dimensions, failure thresholds, memory-management rules, and exact splits are missing, and the abstract's Code field contains no link.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence. SOM takes 0.183 seconds per image in Table 2, while Table 3 reports 98 ms for tracking with TOM. Neither establishes the claimed real-time end-to-end recovery performance without accounting for segmentation and FoundationPose re-registration. Appendix E reports another SOM timing of 0.265 seconds with language conditioning, without reconciling the measurement scope or caching assumptions.

Originality and limitations: Most components use established attention, normalization, segmentation, and pose-estimation machinery; combining Tversky and focal losses alone does not substantiate the claimed novel loss. The ablations do not adequately isolate hierarchical fusion against comparable simpler multi-view architectures. The conclusion offers future directions but little analysis of failure cases or operating limits. No material research-ethics violation is evident; the rejection is driven by unresolved methodological and evidential issues.

strengths: Significance: Automatic initialization and recovery from tracking failure address practical weaknesses of 6D pose systems. Integrating segmentation, FoundationPose, and a memory-based failure detector could reduce manual intervention in robotic deployment.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports substantial improvements over CNOS + FoundationPose, including LM-O AR increasing from 0.41 to 0.53. Table 3 reports tracking AR improving from 50.09 to 67.85 on modified YCB-Video. Segmentation experiments span five BOP datasets.

Presentation and originality: Figure 2 clearly communicates the pipeline. The combination of multi-view attention, semantic conditioning, and learned tracking verification is a useful system-level contribution. Appendix E includes relevant ablations of language conditioning, attention depth, and backbone fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Soundness—central supervision claims are unsupported. SOM is described as entirely label-free and trained exclusively on unlabeled RGB frames, yet Equation 2 requires pixel-level targets and Appendix D repeatedly uses corresponding masks without explaining their provenance or any pseudo-labeling procedure. TOM explicitly uses BOP ground-truth masks (Section 4 and Appendix F). Annotation-free deployment is plausible, but the broader self-supervised and supervision-free claims are not established.

Reproducibility—training specifications materially contradict each other. Section 4 specifies AdamW for both modules and 15 TOM epochs; Appendix D specifies SGD for SOM and Adam with 10 epochs for TOM. The main text uses Tversky and focal losses with weights 1.0 and 0.2, whereas Appendix D specifies different weights and additional Dice and IoU losses. These discrepancies prevent identifying the configuration responsible for the reported results.

Evaluation validity and generalization are insufficiently established. Appendix C trains SOM on datasets that also supply evaluation objects, without reporting an object-disjoint experiment supporting novel-object generalization. TOM’s 200,000 training pairs are described, but its classification evaluation split and safeguards against shared source frames or sequences are unspecified. This does not demonstrate leakage, but leaves the claimed generalization difficult to assess.

Metric and comparison reporting require correction. Appendix B defines AP as an average of precision across IoU thresholds, omitting precision–recall integration; it is unclear whether this is merely a notation error or reflects the implementation. Leaderboard baseline versions and matching evaluation conditions are insufficiently documented. The claim of state-of-the-art segmentation on four datasets contradicts Table 2: STORM leads on three, and its T-LESS score of 47.1 is below several listed methods. Pose comparisons are limited to CNOS + FoundationPose and ground-truth-mask initialization.

Tracking evidence does not fully establish reliable recovery. Random frame dropping and occlusion masks are used without their severity distributions or reproducible settings. Classification accuracy is reported without false-alarm rates, missed failures, recovery success, or recovery latency. Same-object matching can accept an incorrect 6D orientation, so the classifier’s relationship to pose failure needs direct evaluation. A baseline using simple failure detection and the same re-registration mechanism would better isolate TOM’s contribution.

Real-time performance is not demonstrated for the complete system. SOM takes 183 ms in Table 2 and 265 ms with language conditioning in Table 5; tracking takes 98 ms in Table 3. These may suit some applications, but the manuscript does not reconcile the timings or report complete initialization and recovery costs, including segmentation, pose registration, and reference preparation.

Originality, limitations, and reproducibility remain underdeveloped. The contribution primarily integrates established components, and the ablations do not isolate the benefits of the particular hierarchical attention design against comparable alternatives. Important limitations—training supervision, unseen-object performance, appearance-versus-pose verification, and recovery costs—are not adequately discussed. Code and dataset release are promised, but the supplied manuscript provides no usable code link. No material research-ethics concern is evident; the decisive concerns are technical support and reproducibility.

strengths: Significance: Explicit failure detection and automatic re-localization address a useful practical weakness of pose trackers. Combining reference-conditioned segmentation with a learned verifier is a plausible approach to improving autonomous tracking.

Empirical merits: The reported improvements are substantial: Table 2 reports mean segmentation AP of 67.7 versus 56.8 for the strongest listed annotation-free baseline, and Table 4 reports tracking AR increasing from 50.09 to 67.85. Keeping FoundationPose fixed in the mask-source comparison helps isolate segmentation quality.

Presentation and methodological transparency: The paper clearly identifies inherited versus trainable components and correctly explains that the energy-like score is simply a negated BCE-trained logit. Reference-count, language-conditioning, attention-depth, and runtime studies provide useful supporting analysis.

Limitations and ethics: The paper explicitly acknowledges overlap between training and evaluation object identities, reconstruction dependence, and limited coverage of difficult materials. These are appropriate disclosures. The described benchmark research raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—CAD-free metric pose estimation is not established. Appendix G.2 estimates scale, rotation, and translation against the benchmark CAD mesh, then supplies the aligned reconstruction to FoundationPose before inference. This supplies geometric information beyond a post-hoc coordinate conversion. Table 3's ADD-S AUC increases from 44.92 to 99.12 after alignment, but the experiment does not separate coordinate-convention effects from the benefit of CAD-derived scale. A self-consistent coordinate frame alone does not establish correct metric scale. The central deployment claim needs an evaluation with independently recovered scale and benchmark-coordinate conversion applied only for scoring.

Soundness—comparisons do not isolate generalization or architectural gains. SOM is trained with annotated BOP training data containing benchmark object identities, whereas several prominent comparison methods target novel objects. The paper honestly defines its narrower inference setting, but grouping methods by absence of test-time adaptation does not control training supervision, object exposure, backbone, or data volume. Matched-training comparisons are needed to attribute the large Table 2 gains to HSFA. Moreover, the main segmentation evaluation uses rendered references; equivalent performance from an ordinary reference photograph without curated CAD assets is not demonstrated.

Soundness—tracking recovery evidence is incomplete. Table 4 compares against FoundationPose without recovery, but lacks periodic re-registration and simpler verifier baselines using the same recovery backend and temporal policy. Appendix H.4 evaluates only mild corruption: 10% frame dropping and occasional rectangles covering 10–20% of the object bounding box. This does not substantiate reliable recovery from severe occlusion or rapid viewpoint change. Detection delay, false resets, recovery success, and performance across corruption severities are missing. Synthetic crop compatibility also does not directly test incorrect 6D poses that still crop the correct object.

Originality: HSFA combines established self-attention, cross-attention, and feature modulation; TOM combines binary verification with EMA and persistence thresholding. Such integration can be valuable, but the ablations do not establish a distinctive technical advance. The HSFA0 comparison lacks a clearly specified, capacity-matched cross-attention baseline, and its approximately 95% AP results are not reconciled with the main BOP results. The energy terminology adds no separate modeling contribution, as the manuscript itself acknowledges.

Evaluation and presentation contain consequential ambiguities. Appendix B defines AP as an average of precision values across IoU thresholds without describing integration over recall, leaving implementation of the claimed standard metric unclear. Table 3 labels VSD as higher-is-better without explaining whether it represents recall rather than VSD error. Section 4.1 says STORM exactly matches the ground-truth-mask setup on YCB-V, contrary to Table 1. Runtime comparisons also lack matched hardware and workload accounting: Table 4 reports 98 ms per frame, while Appendix E reports 25–33 FPS for steady-state tracking. These measurements may concern different conditions, but the distinction and recovery costs need clearer quantification.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite useful appendix details. Missing specifications include exact training/validation partitions and dataset mixtures, base SOM training and total schedule, backbone variants and attention dimensions, the aggregation of pairwise TOM outputs over its 16-entry memory, and reference-image and sensor-input protocols for the pose experiments. TOM evaluation split construction is particularly important for excluding shared-frame or shared-pair leakage. These omissions, together with the unresolved evaluation issues above, prevent confidently reproducing and building on the central claims.

strengths: Significance: Explicit failure detection and re-localization address a useful practical weakness of local 6D pose trackers. Integrating reference-conditioned segmentation with a learned verifier is a plausible contribution to autonomous tracking.

Empirical merits: The reported improvements are substantial: Table 2 gives 67.7 mean segmentation AP versus 56.8 for NOCTIS, and Table 4 improves tracking AR from 50.09 to 67.85. Holding FoundationPose fixed in the mask-source comparison helps isolate segmentation quality.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper distinguishes frozen foundation components from trainable modules, supplies HSFA pseudocode, and describes losses, augmentations, threshold calibration, and memory management. Reference-count, language-conditioning, and attention-depth ablations provide useful diagnostics.

Limitations and ethics: The authors explicitly acknowledge overlapping training/test object identities, reconstruction dependence, and limited coverage of difficult materials. These disclosures appropriately constrain interpretation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—CAD-free evaluation: Appendix G.2 estimates scale, rotation, and translation against the benchmark CAD mesh and feeds the resulting aligned mesh into FoundationPose. This supplies benchmark geometry before inference, rather than merely converting predicted poses afterward for scoring. Table 3 improves ADD-S AUC from 44.92 to 99.12 with this procedure, but does not separate coordinate-convention effects from the benefit of supplied metric scale. Moreover, the main segmentation evaluation uses rendered references without establishing equivalent performance from ordinary photographs or reconstructed-mesh references. The central single-image, CAD-free deployment claim therefore lacks a convincing end-to-end evaluation.

Soundness—comparison and generalization: SOM is trained with labeled data from the benchmark datasets, and the same object identities may occur during training and testing. Calling inference annotation/adaptation-free does not establish comparable training supervision to the reference-based baselines in Table 2. The disclosed setting is legitimate, but matched-training comparisons or held-out-object experiments are needed to attribute the gains to the proposed architecture and substantiate generalization claims.

Soundness—failure detection and recovery: Appendix H.4 evaluates only mild corruption: 10% independent frame dropping and, on 10% of frames, rectangles covering 10–20% of the object bounding-box area. This does not adequately establish recovery from severe occlusion or rapid viewpoint changes. Table 4 compares against tracking without recovery, but omits periodic reinitialization and simpler detectors using the same recovery backend. Recovery success, detection delay, false-alarm frequency, and pose-based failure labels are also missing. Synthetic identity/crop compatibility is an incomplete proxy for 6D pose validity.

Evaluation definitions and consistency: Appendix B.3 defines AP as an average of precision values across IoU thresholds, omitting precision–recall integration. Table 3 labels VSD as higher-is-better without defining the transformation from an error to a score. Table 8 reports 94.6–95.4 AP under the stated BOP training protocol without explaining its relationship to Table 2's 67.7 AP. These ambiguities affect the interpretation and reproducibility of the central results. Section 4.1 also incorrectly states that STORM exactly matches the ground-truth-mask setup on YCB-V, whereas Table 1 shows lower values on every metric.

Originality: HSFA combines established self-attention, cross-attention, and feature modulation; TOM uses standard BCE classification followed by temporal thresholding. The paper correctly acknowledges that negating the logit is not a new energy-learning objective. The principal originality is therefore system integration, but the ablations do not establish the advantage of hierarchical fusion over a comparably sized conventional attention architecture.

Reproducibility and efficiency: The code-availability footnote contains no usable link. Important details remain unspecified, including the base SOM training schedule, precise TOM evaluation splits, and how pairwise crop scores are aggregated over the 16-entry memory pool. Table 2 compares H100 timings against baseline timings without establishing matched hardware or workloads. Table 4 reports 98 ms per frame, while Appendix E reports a 25–33 FPS steady-state loop; these settings need reconciliation, and initialization/recovery latency needs direct measurement.

strengths: Significance: Explicit failure detection and automatic re-localization address a useful weakness of local 6D pose trackers. Integrating segmentation, reconstructed geometry, and a learned verifier is a practically motivated contribution.

Empirical merits: The reported gains are substantial. SOM achieves 67.7 mean AP versus 56.8 for the strongest listed annotation-free baseline (Table 2), and STORM improves stress-test ADD-S AUC from 66.76 to 88.56 (Table 4). Holding FoundationPose fixed in the mask comparison is a useful experimental control.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper distinguishes frozen components from trainable modules and provides attention pseudocode, loss settings, augmentation details, threshold calibration, and component runtime measurements. It explicitly acknowledges that the negative-logit score is not a separately trained energy model.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations appropriately acknowledge overlapping train/test object identities, reconstruction dependencies, and restricted material coverage. These disclosures are helpful. The described benchmark research raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—CAD-free deployment is not established by the main geometry experiment. Appendix G.2 fits scale, rotation, and translation against the benchmark CAD mesh and supplies the aligned mesh to FoundationPose. This changes inference geometry, rather than merely converting predictions for evaluation. Table 3's ADD-S AUC rises from 44.92 to 99.12 after alignment. Coordinate alignment is understandable for benchmarking, but the experiment does not separate coordinate convention from privileged metric-scale information. A CAD-independent scale procedure and end-to-end evaluation from a real reference photograph are needed; Table 2 instead uses rendered references.

Soundness—recovery attribution is incomplete. Table 4 compares the full recovery system against FoundationPose without recovery, but does not compare periodic re-initialization, cosine-triggered recovery, or TOM without attention under the same temporal policy. Table 5 evaluates synthetic crop compatibility rather than actual pose failures; an incorrect pose can retain the correct object identity and crop. Failure precision/recall, detection delay, recovery success, and pose-error-based failure labels are needed to substantiate the verifier's tracking-validity claims.

Evaluation scope and fairness: The severe-occlusion and rapid-motion claims exceed the documented quantitative stress test. Appendix H.4 uses 10% independent frame dropping and occasional rectangles covering 10–20% of the object bounding-box area. There is no severity sweep or prolonged disappearance test. SOM also trains on the evaluated BOP object identities, whereas the comparison does not establish matched training-data access for reference-based baselines. The disclosed adaptation-free definition is legitimate, but these results do not isolate generalization to unseen objects.

Originality: HSFA combines established self-attention, cross-attention, and language-conditioned normalization; TOM combines BCE classification with EMA and persistence thresholding. A useful systems contribution remains possible, but the ablations do not convincingly identify what the hierarchy contributes beyond a capacity-matched standard fusion model. The HSFA0 baseline is loosely specified, and Table 8's approximately 95% AP is not reconciled with the main benchmark's 67.7 AP.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details remain missing, including SOM training duration and base-checkpoint preparation, exact model variants and attention dimensions, aggregation of pairwise TOM predictions across the 16-entry memory, and precise verification train/validation/test splits. Depth and camera-calibration requirements for FoundationPose are not specified. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the claimed single-image pipeline.

Presentation and measurement consistency: Appendix B defines AP as an average of precision values over IoU thresholds without specifying precision–recall integration, and Table 3 labels VSD as higher-is-better without defining the reported transformation. Section 4.1 says STORM exactly matches the ground-truth-mask setup, although Table 1 does not. Runtime comparisons also need a common accounting basis: Table 4 reports 98 ms per frame, Appendix E reports 25–33 FPS steady-state tracking, and Table 2 compares H100 SOM timings against leaderboard runtimes without establishing matched hardware or per-object versus per-image scope. These ambiguities materially weaken confidence in the accuracy and efficiency claims.
